lead: A DAO is an organisation whose rules, treasury and decisions live in smart contracts and token votes, with no board in the middle. GHOST is a fork-choice rule that follows the heaviest block subtree instead of the longest chain, so stale blocks still count. A side chain is a separate blockchain joined to a main chain by a bridge. Only a few universities teach this chapter; the ideas appear in DeFi governance, Ethereum's uncle blocks and scaling side chains.
prereq: You need: Unit 3 forks and consensus, and 5.1 Ethereum network.

sections.h3: DAO: rules and votes in code

blocks.text: A DAO (decentralised autonomous organisation) is a group whose membership, treasury and rules sit in smart contracts. Governance tokens give voting rights. Anyone may submit a proposal: a call to a contract function with arguments. A vote needs a quorum and a majority, and a timelock delays execution so members can leave before a change lands.

The DAO, launched in 2016, held a large ether treasury. Its split function sent ether to the caller before setting that caller's balance to zero. An attacker re-entered split through a fallback function and repeated the withdrawal inside one transaction. This is reentrancy: an external call made before the state update. The chain was hard forked to return the funds, splitting Ethereum and Ethereum Classic.

Other contract attacks: integer overflow, missing access control on admin functions, front-running of trades, and price-oracle manipulation. Defences are the checks-effects-interactions order, reentrancy guards, audited libraries and a pause switch.

GHOST (Greedy Heaviest Observed SubTree) is a fork-choice rule. Short block times create many blocks at one height; longest-chain throws all but one away. GHOST follows the branch whose subtree holds the most blocks, so stale work still counts.

blocks.where: weight(b) is the number of blocks in b's subtree including b itself; c ranges over the direct children of b; Σ is their sum.

items: Compute weights bottom-up: a leaf has weight 1.
Move to the child with the larger weight.
Repeat until a leaf; that path is the main chain.

blocks.text: Ethereum uses a GHOST-based rule, so orphaned blocks become uncles: a later block names them and they earn a partial reward, which protects miners against network latency.

A side chain is a separate blockchain with its own consensus and validators, joined to a main chain by a bridge. In a two-way peg, users lock coins in a main-chain contract, the bridge mints the same amount on the side chain, and burning on exit unlocks the original.

The side chain does not inherit mainnet security. Its validators can reorg or halt it, and the bridge contract holding the locked coins becomes the target. Federated bridges rely on a multisig of known signers; trustless bridges verify the other chain's headers. Both add attack surface. Rollups differ: they post data or proofs back to the main chain.

figure.caption: Weights are counted bottom-up. B holds four blocks against U1's one, so B is chosen; below B, C holds two against U2's one.

spec.aria: GHOST block tree: D weighs 1, C weighs 2, B weighs 4 against uncle U2's 1, A weighs 6, and the main chain follows A-B-C-D.

examples.question: Blocks form this tree: A is the root. A has children B and U1. B has children C and U2. C has child D. A block's weight is 1 plus the weights of its children. Under GHOST, which child of A and which child of B lie on the main chain? Give every weight.
steps: B has children C and U2: weight(B) = 1 + 2 + 1 = 4.
Children of A: B = 4, U1 = 1, so A moves to B.
Children of B: C = 2, U2 = 1, so B moves to C.
C has only D, so the main chain is A-B-C-D.
examples.answer: A follows B (4 against 1), B follows C (2 against 1); the main chain is A-B-C-D, with U1 and U2 as uncles.

traps: GHOST is not longest-chain: it compares subtree weights, not heights.
Weight includes the block itself; forgetting the +1 gives 3 instead of 4 for B.
Uncles are not on the main chain and earn a partial reward, not a full one.
A side chain does not inherit mainnet security; the bridge contract and its signers add risk.
Reentrancy is an ordering bug (external call before the balance update), not a compiler fault.

quiz.q: Define DAO and name two things its contracts hold.
quiz.a: A decentralised autonomous organisation: rules and treasury held in smart contracts, with token holders voting on proposals.

quiz.q: Expand GHOST and state what it selects.
quiz.a: Greedy Heaviest Observed SubTree; it selects the child whose subtree contains the most blocks.

quiz.q: Why does Ethereum pay uncles a partial reward?
quiz.a: Short block times orphan valid blocks through latency; paying uncles keeps miners from losing all work and discourages selfish mining.

quiz.q: Root A has children B (subtree weight 5) and C (weight 2). Which child does GHOST pick, and by what margin?
quiz.a: B, since 5 > 2; the margin is 3 blocks.

quiz.q: Explain how reentrancy drained The DAO in one transaction.
quiz.a: split sent ether before zeroing the caller's balance; the fallback re-entered split, so the same balance was withdrawn repeatedly before any update.

quiz.q: A side chain runs five validators and a 3-of-5 multisig bridge. State two security limits.
quiz.a: Three validators can finalise false blocks, and three signers can release locked main-chain coins; neither needs mainnet consensus.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production DAOs now split voting from execution with timelocks and delegate voting, and bridge hacks have become the largest losses in the field. Ethereum's fork choice has moved toward LMD-GHOST, which weights by attestations rather than block count, and rollups carry most scaling work. Search next: LMD-GHOST, optimistic rollup fraud proofs, and bridge designs.
